proof:
# Cap-adjusted inverse sections need not be subadditive

Let K=conv{(-1,-1),(3,-1),(-1,4)} and let the source be zero, an interior point. For a nonzero normal v define

    Q(v)=area(K intersect {v.x>=0}),
    sigma(v)=length(K intersect {v.x=0})/||v||,
    h(v)=sqrt(Q(v))/sigma(v).

The following exact values result by intersecting the three triangle edges with the cutting line and using the determinant area formula:

| v | Q(v) | sigma(v) | h(v)^2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| (1,-6) | 395/102 | 25/51 | 4029/250 |
| (0,-4) | 18/5 | 4/5 | 45/8 |
| (1,-10) | 1019/270 | 41/135 | 137565/3362 |

Write a,b,c for the three entries in the last column. Then

    r=c-a-b=32235879/1681000>0,
    r^2-4ab=14502698692641/2825761000000>0.

Thus r>2sqrt(ab), so sqrt(c)>sqrt(a)+sqrt(b). Since the third normal is the sum of the first two, h is not subadditive. Replacing raw areas by normalized cap fractions scales every h by the same positive constant and leaves the counterexample unchanged.

This rejects an asymmetric norm shortcut to the general joint-row inequality. It neither contradicts the joint-row inequality for actual simplex cap circuits nor invalidates Busemann's theorem for centrally symmetric bodies. The three displayed cuts are not being presented as a balanced isolated-vertex circuit.
